contract.question: Quais são os trade-offs entre busca lexical e busca híbrida?
contract.objective: analisar as diferenças e implicações de custo/benefício entre busca lexical e híbrida.
assumptions: busca lexical refere-se a busca por correspondência de strings (termos, frases, n-gramas) em um índice.
busca híbrida é a combinação de busca lexical com métodos de similaridade semântica (vetores, embeddings, TF-IDF, BM25).
trade-offs envolvem precisão, recall, latência e complexidade de implementação.
a pergunta não se refere a sistemas de busca específicos (ex: Lucene, ElasticSearch) ou a algoritmos de ranking (ex: Reciprocal Rank Fusion).
sufficiency_criteria: responder a pergunta com base nas questões acima.
abordar os trade-offs de precisão/recall, latência e complexidade.
comparar a abordagem lexical pura com a híbrida.

questions.sufficiency: o material explica as distinções teóricas entre os dois métodos.

questions.sufficiency: o material detalha os ganhos e perdas de cada abordagem.

questions.question: Como a busca híbrida mitiga as limitações da busca lexical?
questions.sufficiency: o material explica como a combinação melhora a precisão e a recuperação.

sources.title: What is hybrid search? How it works and when to use it
Hybrid RAG: Lexical Search and Semantic Search Explained
Lexical vs. Semantic Search in Data Architectures | Aerospike
Hybrid Search Implementation: Vector and Keyword Retrieval | Unstructured

evidence.quote: Hybrid search is an information retrieval technique that blends two or more search methods (e.g., lexical search and semantic search) into a single ranked list to improve relevance and recall.
The most common pairing combines full-text lexical search, which is great at matching exact words and phrases, with semantic vector search, which interprets the meaning behind a query.
Lexical search is ideal when you have well-structured data and users know what they are looking for.
Because it has no model overhead, lexical search is fast and efficient, with filters and facets that perform reliably even at scale without slowdowns or full index scans.
the semantic side provides a deep understanding of the user's underlying intent.
hybrid search can unite other approaches — like geospatial + semantic search or even text + image search — to fit different needs.
Lexical methods (including full-text search) match tokens precisely. They only succeed when the query and document share vocabulary.
Lexical search has been part of information systems for decades.
Early workloads depended on deterministic matching.
Most queries issued by databases and other internal tools referenced exact terms like IDs or error codes.
For example, a SQL query using LIKE '%error%' searches for any text containing the substring "error".
Modern lexical search is much more advanced and determines relevance based on token presence and frequency.
Documents are scored higher when query terms appear more frequently or are rarer across the entire corpus.
Most lexical search implementations use inverted indexes.
Semantic methods capture intended meaning, but are poorly suited for exact identifiers (IDs, numbers, proper names) that lexical systems handle precisely.
Lexical search matches a query against an index of stored text.
This approach is rule-based and predictable because it uses exact words or simple variations of them within a text to decide what results to return.
Lexical retrieval systems have served as the industry standard for decades because they’re precise for structured data and exact keyword matches by using inverted indexes.

Conversely, semantic search uses natural language processing and vector search to interpret the contextual meaning of user queries, helping a search engine return relevant information even if the query didn’t use the exact words.
Learn about BM25 scoring, vector embeddings, infrastructure costs, and why hybrid search is the industry standard.
The transition from traditional keyword matching to intent-based semantic search changes how organizations manage information retrieval.
Enterprises usually use lexical retrieval to search structured data such as product codes, identifiers, or technical documentation where the user is looking for an exact keyword.
First, data needs to be analyzed and undergo tokenization, where raw text is broken down into individual basic terms, followed by normalization techniques such as stemming or lemmatization.
Hybrid search is a retrieval approach that combines lexical search and vector search in one pipeline.
Lexical search is keyword-based retrieval that scores documents using term frequency signals, often through BM25 and an inverted index.
Vector search is embedding-based retrieval that represents text as vectors and ranks by similarity in a vector index.
Hybrid search runs both retrieval methods and then merges the results into a single ranked list.
This means you reduce the chance that a query fails because it needed either strict keywords or broader meaning.
